summary:
Paraguay has no legal gender recognition procedure in force. The judiciary has yet to issue final rulings in ten lawsuits filed by trans people seeking recognition of their legal names, among them cases brought by Yren Rotela and Mariana Sepúlveda that have been pending since 2016. Both plaintiffs have taken communications to the UN Human Rights Committee under the Optional Protocol to the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights and are awaiting a decision. A 1993 civil court case seeking to register Ramón Fidel, who had undergone gender reassignment surgery, as a woman ended without a decision because Fidel died in a traffic accident before judgment. Trans people are not permitted to change their name or gender on official documents, so a trans visitor whose passport marker conflicts with their presentation has no domestic route to alignment.

Amnesty International's 2025-26 reporting records that two trans migrants were denied identity documents, and that Asunción's city council banned an event honouring a trans human-rights defender who died in March. The same reporting counts 37 registered feminicides in 2025 and notes an April bill to merge the Ministry of Women into a Ministry of the Family.

Discrimination, harassment and gender-based violence push trans women out of their hometowns into migration and sex work, according to AP reporting from September 2025.

There is no broad anti-discrimination law. A November 2015 bill to ban discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity has not advanced since introduction. Protections that do exist are narrow and sector-specific: Law 5162/2014 requires that collective dormitory placement for adolescents take account of age, sexual orientation and degree of psychic development; Decree 6973 under Law 577/2016 protects women from violence without discrimination based on sexual orientation; Law 6149/2018 bars discrimination against stateless persons on grounds including gender identity; Law 6534/2020 treats sexual orientation data as sensitive personal data; and Article 28 of the Ministry of Public Defense's internal rules prohibits sexual-orientation discrimination against its employees.

Two health-sector instruments address trans people directly. Resolution 695, approved by the Ministry of Public Health and Social Welfare in October 2016, requires that trans people be able to use their social name on medical records, medical history and forms, and that health service officials in the Integrated Networks of Health Services treat patients using that identified social name. Law 7018 on Mental Health, enacted 15 November 2022, provides in Article 3 that a mental-health diagnosis may in no case be made on the exclusive basis of sexual choice, sexual orientation or gender identity.

In October 2017 the government implemented a ban on discussion of LGBT issues in public schools; the Minister of Education stated at the time that it might consider burning books that raise awareness about transgender people. A ruling-party figure, Horacio Cartes, was reported in October 2017 as saying he would 'shoot himself in the testicles' if his son married another man, later apologising to those offended.

Same-sex sexual activity has been legal since 1990. Since 1992 the Constitution has limited marriage, de facto unions and the family to one man and one woman under Articles 49 to 52, and Article 140 of the Civil Code expressly prohibits marriage between persons of the same sex. The Inter-American Court of Human Rights' advisory opinion of 8 January 2018 holds that states party to the American Convention must grant same-sex couples access to domestic family registration systems including marriage; Paraguay is an OAS party and therefore bound by the ruling, while its domestic law recognises neither same-sex marriage nor unions, leaving local law lagging behind the opinion. A lawsuit relying on that opinion to recognise same-sex marriage remains pending. A trans visitor in a relationship read locally as same-sex therefore has no route to recognition in Paraguay.

Under the Adoption Law 1136/97, single persons of any sex may adopt regardless of marital status; the statute's prohibitions cover only infectious disease, mental disorders or child-abuse records, and it does not explicitly bar same-sex couples or singles from adopting, though equal preference is given to opposite-sex marriages and de facto unions and to single women.

There is no official prohibition on gay, lesbian or bisexual people entering the Armed Forces or National Police, after the Chamber of Deputies rejected a bill to that effect in June 2010 by 42 votes to 4.
tangentialFactors:
During the Stroessner dictatorship (1954-1989) LGBT people faced heavy persecution. In the 1 September 1959 Case 108, police arrested and tortured 108 gay men in Asunción over a fire and made their names public, and the government publicly encouraged hatred and violence against LGBT people. The most recent documented incident in this record is from 2025: Amnesty International's 2025-26 reporting on the banned Asunción event honouring a trans human-rights defender who died in March.

Reports of violence and discrimination against LGBT community members are described as frequent and often ignored by the police. The Catholic Church retains strong influence and has opposed measures to improve LGBT lives, alongside a rise in religious fundamentalism that has concerned LGBT advocacy groups. A Pew survey conducted 26 November 2013 to 8 January 2014 found 15% support for same-sex marriage with 81% opposed; the 2017 AmericasBarometer recorded 26% support. These attitude and polling figures refer to LGBT people or same-sex marriage generally, not to trans people specifically.

Raw-count context: Amnesty International's figure of 37 registered feminicides in 2025 is a raw count with no per-capita denominator supplied, and the source does not rank Paraguay against other jurisdictions on this measure.

Ten lawsuits filed by trans people for legal name recognition remain undecided, including the Rotela and Sepúlveda cases filed in December 2016 invoking Article 25 of the Constitution on free expression and construction of identity and Article 42 of the Civil Code on change of first name; both plaintiffs' communications to the UN Human Rights Committee under the ICCPR Optional Protocol are awaiting decision.

In health care, Resolution 695 of October 2016 entitles trans people to use their social name on medical records, medical history and forms, and obliges officials in the Integrated Networks of Health Services to treat patients using that social name. Law 7018 on Mental Health of 15 November 2022, Article 3, bars any mental-health diagnosis being made on the exclusive basis of sexual choice, sexual orientation or gender identity, and grounds mental-health care in non-discrimination on those grounds.

Two trans migrants were denied identity documents, according to Amnesty International's 2025-26 reporting. An April bill would merge the Ministry of Women into a Ministry of the Family. In October 2017 the government banned discussion of LGBT issues in public schools.

Residents in what would be locally classed as a same-sex relationship cannot marry: Articles 49-52 of the Constitution and Article 140 of the Civil Code bar it, and a lawsuit relying on the Inter-American Court's 8 January 2018 advisory opinion remains pending. Adoption is open to single persons of any sex under Law 1136/97.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the UN Human Rights Committee has issued a decision on the Rotela and Sepúlveda communications is unresolved in this record; the sources state only that a decision is awaited.

The fate of the November 2015 anti-discrimination bill after introduction is not sourced beyond its failure to advance. The current status of the April bill to merge the Ministry of Women into a Ministry of the Family is not sourced.

No entry, visa or border-screening rules specific to trans travellers, and no rules on gender markers in foreign passports at entry, are documented in this inventory; those questions are not sourced here.

The 37 feminicides recorded in 2025 are not disaggregated by whether any victim was trans, and no trans-specific homicide figure with a denominator appears in the inventory.
